title: Tvam agne dyubhiḥ: Agni born from waters, stone, woods and plants
theme: A Vedic verse to Agni: he flares up quickly and is born from the waters, the stone, the woods and the plants, pure among men.

words.context: the anonymous commentator: «द्युभिरुत्तमकान्तिभिः» — with excellent splendours
the anonymous commentator: «त्वमाशु शीघ्रं शोषयति भक्तानां पापमित्याशुशुक्षणिः» — you quickly dry up the sins of devotees
the anonymous commentator: among the sacrificers («यजमानानां मध्ये»)
the anonymous commentator: «सर्वपदार्थभुगपि सन्सर्वदा शुचिरेव» — though he consumes all things, always pure

sandhi.rule: tvam + agne: the m is joined to the vowel.
dyubhiḥ + tvam → dyubhis tvam: the visarga becomes s before t.
aśmanaḥ + pari → aśmanas pari: in Vedic texts the visarga before p is written s.

sandhi.type: final m before a vowel; visarga before t
sandhi.rule: tvam + oṣadhībhyaḥ: the m is joined to the vowel; oṣadhībhyaḥ + tvam → oṣadhībhyas tvam.

morphology.note: One word, though the base prints it with a space (आशु शुक्षणिः). The anonymous commentator derives it from āśu ‘quickly’ and śuṣ ‘dry up’; the edition reports his derivation.
Ablative singular of aśman ‘stone’ with the postposition pari, ‘out of the stone’; the visarga is written s before pari.
Middle present of √jan, ‘you are born’; the ablatives give where from.

translation.literal: You, O Agni, with the days; you, quickly flaring; you from the waters, you out of the stone; you from the woods, you from the plants; you, O lord of men, are born bright among men.
translation.readable: You, Agni, with the days; you flare up quickly; you are born from the waters, from the stone, from the woods and the plants; you, lord of men, are born pure among men.

anvaya: अग्ने नृपते त्वम् द्युभिः । त्वम् आशुशुक्षणिः । त्वम् अद्भ्यः । त्वम् अश्मनः परि । त्वम् वनेभ्यः । त्वम् ओषधीभ्यः । त्वम् नृणाम् शुचिः जायसे
syntax: A litany of seven ‘you’ clauses addressed to Agni (vocatives agne, nṛpate). One verb, jāyase, ‘you are born’, closes the series and is understood with the ablatives of origin before it (adbhyaḥ, aśmanaḥ pari, vanebhyaḥ, oṣadhībhyaḥ); śuciḥ is its predicate.

ambiguities.note: With jāyase they say where Agni is born from. The anonymous commentator reads them otherwise: above the waters, on the stone of Meru («महामेरुरूपस्य पाषाणस्य पर्युपरि तिष्ठसि»), in the woods, pervading the plants, taking the cases as exchanged.
The anonymous commentator construes the whole verse with the request of the previous anuvāka, ‘protect me from death’ («मृत्योः सकाशान्मां पाहीति पूर्वेणान्वयः»).

metre.name: irregular
metre.note: As printed the two lines count 20 and 20 syllables. No commentary in the edition’s sources names the metre, and the edition does not resolve semivowels to fit one.

beginner: This is an old Vedic verse to Agni, the god of fire. It repeats ‘you’ seven times and lists the places fire comes from: it flares up quickly, it is born from the waters, from stone, from the woods and from the plants, and among people it is born pure. The verse names the many places where fire is found or kindled. The only commentator in this edition who explains it, the anonymous one, reads it as continuing the previous line, which asked for protection from death: Agni too is asked to protect. He explains the epithets: Agni quickly dries up the sins of his devotees, and stays pure though he consumes everything. The edition reports this as his reading.
analogy: Like a list of all the places a river is found — in the mountain spring, in the clouds, in the sea: one water, many births.

commentary.label: direct
commentary.text: It addresses Agni seven times as ‘you’: with the days, quickly flaring, from the waters, out of the stone, from the woods, from the plants; and as lord of men, born pure among men.

commentary.q: Why is it here, according to the commentator?
commentary.label: traditional
commentary.text: The anonymous commentator joins it to the preceding formula: Agni, with all these powers, is asked to protect from death («एवंविधप्रभावस्त्वं मृत्योः सकाशान्मां पाहीति पूर्वेणान्वयः»). He explains āśuśukṣaṇi as one who quickly dries up the devotees’ sin, and the purity of fire: «वैदिकलौकिकश्मशानिकसर्वपदार्थभुगपि सन्सर्वदा शुचिरेव» — though he consumes everything, of the rite, of the world and of the cremation ground, he is always pure.

commentary.label: traditional
commentary.text: For the waters the anonymous commentator gives a reason from scripture: fire is prior to water, since water comes from fire, and he cites «अग्नेरापः» as śruti. He reads ‘stone’ as Meru, on whose peaks the gods dwell. These readings are his.

commentary.q: What is unusual in the wording?
commentary.label: linguistic
commentary.text: The visarga of aśmanaḥ is written s before pari (aśmanas pari), a Vedic sandhi. The base prints āśuśukṣaṇiḥ with a space, as आशु शुक्षणिः.

schools.disagreement: No Vedānta-school commentary on this text is in the edition’s sources: Raṅgarāmānuja’s is not available, and the commentaries present (the anonymous bhāṣya, Sāyaṇa, Bhaṭṭa Bhāskara) are ritual and Vedic explanations, not school readings. Only the anonymous commentator explains this verse in the edition’s sources.

contemporary.text: The verse looks for fire everywhere — in water, stone, wood and plant — and finds one thing in many places. Noticing the same thing at work in very different settings is a way of seeing connections. This is a modern reflection on the passage, not part of its traditional meaning.

reflect.beginner: Where in everyday life do you find fire or warmth hidden in something that does not look like fire?
reflect.deeper: The commentator reads the verse as another plea for protection. What does it add to say whom one is asking, and with what powers?
reflect.practice: Notice today one source of warmth or energy you usually take for granted.

references.text: The verse is also found in the Ṛgveda (2.1.1); the edition’s Ṛgveda source has only the first maṇḍala, so it is not cited as a checked parallel.
No comment of Sāyaṇa or Bhāskara on this anuvāka is in the edition’s files.

flags.note: The Tirupati e-text lacks शुचिः here and prints it at the start of the next anuvāka; the collation leaves it for review. The Ānandāśrama pariśiṣṭa text reads आशुशुक्षाणिः and ओषधिभ्यः, which the collation classes as its errors.
aśmanas pari needs a Vedic visarga rule (visarga written s before p) that the shared sandhi engine does not yet have; reported for the engine.
Only one commentary explains this anuvāka in the edition’s sources.
